front: What is an arbitrage opportunity in the one-period market of Lesson 1?
back: A portfolio θ with cost p·θ ≤ 0, payoff (Xθ)_s ≥ 0 in every state s, and either p·θ < 0 or (Xθ)_s > 0 for some state s (Definition 1.1). A zero-cost portfolio with zero payoff in every state is not one.

front: What is a set of state prices?
back: A vector ψ with ψ_s > 0 for every state s and p_j = Σ_s ψ_s X_sj for every asset j, that is, p = Xᵀψ (Definition 3.1).

front: What does Assumption A3 (no arbitrage) say?
back: No portfolio is an arbitrage opportunity in the market under study (Assumption A3, Section 1).

front: Under A3, do two portfolios with the same payoff in every state have the same cost?
back: Yes, under A3. If Xa = Xb then p·a = p·b (Proposition 2.1). The proof applies A3 to a − b and to b − a, whose payoffs are zero.

front: Under A3, if portfolio a pays at least as much as b in every state, how do their costs compare?
back: p·a ≥ p·b (Proposition 2.2). The result uses A3 and nothing else (Remark 2.3).

front: Do strictly positive state prices exclude arbitrage, and does this need A3?
back: They do, and the claim does not assume A3 (Proposition 3.2). The proof writes p·θ = Σ_s ψ_s (Xθ)_s, a sum of non-negative terms.

front: Does no arbitrage imply that strictly positive state prices exist?
back: Not claimed. Proposition 3.2 runs one way, and Remark 3.3 states that the converse is not claimed.

front: In the market of Example 3.4 at stock price 1, what are the state prices?
back: ψ_u = 1/20 and ψ_d = 17/20. Both are positive and reproduce both prices, so the market has no arbitrage (Example 3.4; Lab 1, Part A).

front: With the bond at 9/10 and the payoffs of Example 3.4, for which stock prices q is there no arbitrage?
back: Exactly for 9/10 < q < 27/10 (Proposition 3.5). At q = 9/10 and at q = 27/10 there is arbitrage, although the state-price formulas give zero there (Remark 3.6).

front: Do state prices add up to one, as probabilities do?
back: No. In the market of Example 3.4 at stock price 1, the state prices 1/20 and 17/20 add to 9/10, the price of the bond that pays 1 in every state (Problem P3). No probabilities are assigned to the states.

front: Does a portfolio that makes money in some state count as an arbitrage?
back: No. Definition 1.1 needs cost at most zero and payoff non-negative in every state. One stock and two short bonds at prices 1 and 9/10 cost −4/5 and pay (1, −1), so the portfolio can lose in state d.

front: At bond price 9/10 and stock price 1/2, which holdings (bond, stock) cost zero?
back: The multiples t(−5, 9) for real t. Each pays t(22, 4), so the payoff is strictly positive in both states exactly when t > 0 (Problem M3).

front: Does a zero count of arbitrage portfolios in a search box establish that a market has no arbitrage?
back: No. The search covers holdings from −10 to 10 of each asset, so the count is a fact about that box. Proposition 3.2 gives the all-holdings result from the positive state prices of Part A, 1/20 and 17/20 (Problem E3).

front: Does Proposition 2.2 order the costs of two portfolios whose payoffs are higher in one state and lower in another?
back: No. It applies only when one payoff is at least the other in every state. For a pair whose payoffs cross, these results determine no cost order (Remark 2.3).

front: What is the payoff at expiry of the long party to a forward contract?
back: The long party pays the forward price F and receives one unit, so its payoff at expiry is S_τ − F. The short party's payoff is F − S_τ (Definition 1.1).

front: What discount factor from date τ back to date 0 does A4 give?
back: e^{−rτ}. A4 fixes one rate r over the life of the contract, continuously compounded, so an amount x at date 0 becomes x e^{rt} at date t (Assumption A4).

front: What is the cost-of-carry forward price?
back: F* = S e^{rτ}: the spot price S compounded at rate r to expiry τ (Definition 2.1).

front: Under A1 to A4 and no arbitrage, what forward price is required?
back: F = F* = S e^{rτ} (Proposition 2.2).

front: Does the no-arbitrage forward price depend on the expected spot price at expiry?
back: No. Under A1 to A4 the proof uses no probability and no expectation of S_τ, so F* is a function of S, r and τ alone (Remark 2.3).

front: An asset costs 50 dollars with no income (A1), r = 0.05 continuously compounded, and τ = 1/2. What is the no-arbitrage forward price?
back: 50e^{0.025} = 51.2658 dollars, which is 51.27 dollars to the cent (Example 2.4). Lab 2, Part A: 5126.58 cents.

front: Is a forward priced above today's spot overpriced when r > 0?
back: Not necessarily. Under A1 to A4, F* = S e^{rτ} exceeds S when r > 0 and τ > 0, and that excess is the cost of carry. Only a price different from F* is a mispricing (Remark 2.5; Section 5, misconception 3).

front: Under A1 to A4 and A3, does a long forward struck at F* pay the same at expiry as one unit of the asset bought at S with a loan of S?
back: Yes, in every state. Both pay S_τ − S e^{rτ}, because F* = S e^{rτ} (proof of Proposition 2.2; Lab 2, Part B).

front: In Lab 2, Part C, what does selling a forward quoted at 5200 cents and buying the asset with a loan earn?
back: 73.42 cents in every expiry state, with zero net cash today. The payoff equals the quote minus the fair price (Lab 2, Part C; Solution E2).

front: Under A1 to A4, and A3 at each date t, what is the value of a long forward with price F held at date t?
back: V_t = S_t − F e^{−r(τ − t)}, under A1 to A4 and A3 at each date t (Proposition 3.1). The proof buys the unit and borrows F e^{−r(τ − t)}.

front: Under A1 to A4, and A3 at each date t, what is the value at inception of a forward priced at F*?
back: Zero at date 0 (Corollary 3.2).

front: In Lab 2, Part E, what is the value to the long side of a forward struck at the fair price, after a quarter year with the spot at 5300 cents?
back: 237.11 cents (Lab 2, Part E): the spot 5300 minus the discounted fair price, computed from the unrounded fair price.

front: If the asset pays one known income I at date t1 and A1 is dropped, with A2 to A4 and A3 kept, what is the no-arbitrage forward price?
back: F = S e^{rτ} − I e^{r(τ − t1)} = (S − I e^{−r t1}) e^{rτ}, under A2 to A4 and A3, with 0 < t1 ≤ τ (Problem P1).

front: Under A3, can two forward contracts on one asset with one expiry have different prices?
back: No. Long the contract with the lower price and short the one with the higher price gives a payoff F2 − F1 > 0 in every state at zero cost, which A3 excludes (Problem P3).

front: Under A1 and A3, with the frictionless parts of A2 and A4 at two rates r_ℓ ≤ r_b, which forward prices admit arbitrage?
back: Under A1 and A3, with A4 at the two rates in place of r, and the frictionless parts of A2 (no transaction costs, free short sales, unrestricted lending and borrowing, and no default risk), a price F outside [S e^{r_ℓ τ}, S e^{r_b τ}] admits arbitrage when r_ℓ ≤ r_b (Problem R1). Whether every price inside the interval is arbitrage-free is not established.

front: Does a buyer of a forward pay a premium at inception?
back: No. Definition 1.1 makes no payment at date 0. The buyer pays the forward price F at expiry, in exchange for the unit.

front: How does a futures contract differ from the forward contract of Lesson 2?
back: A futures contract is standardized and traded on an exchange, where a clearing house stands between the parties. Gains and losses are paid between the parties every day, not only at expiry (Definition 1.1).

front: What is the daily variation margin of a long futures holder?
back: Δ_i = F_i − F_{i−1} per unit, where F_i is the close on day i and F_0 is the entry price. A short holder receives −Δ_i. Crediting these amounts each day is marking to market (Definition 1.2).

front: What does Assumption A8′ assume about the margin account?
back: The margin account earns no interest, and the daily variation margins are the only cash flows of the position (Assumption A8′).

front: Under A8′, what does the margin balance after day i equal?
back: B_i = F_i − F_0 (Proposition 1.3), where B_i is the balance after day i. The balance is the sum of the daily margins through day i.
basis: Proof on the page; Lab 3, Part A (SIMULATED path)

front: Does the margining identity imply that the account can meet margin requirements?
back: No. Margin requirements are not modelled, and the identity holds whatever the requirements are (Remark 1.4).

front: What are the two legs of an interest-rate swap, and what does the payer of the fixed leg pay and receive?
back: The fixed leg pays R per unit of notional at each date i. The floating leg pays the coupon L_i for period i, set at date i − 1. The payer pays R and receives L_i (Definition 3.1).

front: What does the single-curve assumption A8 say about the floating coupon?
back: One set of discount factors both discounts the payments and sets the floating coupons, so 1 + L_i = DF_{i-1} / DF_i, and every DF_i is strictly positive for i = 1 to n (Assumption A8).

front: Under A8, what is the present value of the floating leg per unit of notional?
back: 1 − DF_n (Proposition 3.2). The coupon at date i has present value DF_{i−1} − DF_i, and the sum telescopes because DF_0 = 1.

front: Under A8, what is the par rate of a swap?
back: R_par = (1 − DF_n) / Σ_{i=1}^{n} DF_i, the unique fixed rate at which the swap has zero value at date 0 (Proposition 3.3).

front: On a flat curve with DF_i = (1 + ρ)^{−i}, what is the par rate?
back: The flat rate ρ (Example 3.4).

front: Under A8, what is the value to the fixed payer at a fixed rate K per unit of notional?
back: (R_par − K) Σ_i DF_i under A8. It is positive when K < R_par, zero when K = R_par, and negative when K > R_par (Proposition 3.5).

front: On the 1,000,000-dollar notional of Lab 3, Part B, what is the value to the payer of a swap struck one percentage point above the par rate, in cents?
back: −h Σ_i DF_i with h one percentage point, which is −4415468 cents (Problem P2; Lab 3, Part B).

front: If the margin account earns a constant rate η per day, what is the balance after n days?
back: B_n = Σ_{i=1}^{n} Δ_i (1 + η)^{n−i} (Problem P3).

front: Do a long futures position and a forward with the same expiry pay their gains and losses on the same dates?
back: No. A futures position pays its daily variation margins, which sum to F_n − F_0 under A8′ (Proposition 1.3). A forward pays once, at expiry (Definition 1.1 of Lesson 2). The lesson does not compare the two totals (Remark 1.5).

front: Does the futures buyer pay the futures price up front?
back: Not in this model. The position costs nothing to enter, and the only cash flows are the daily variation margins. The collateral a clearing house requires is outside the model (Remark 1.4).
basis: Lesson 3, Section 5 (misconception 2) and Remark 1.4; model convention, A8′

front: Is the par rate of a swap the market's interest rate?
back: No. Under A8, R_par is the ratio of Proposition 3.3, which uses all the discount factors, and it equals none of the typed-in zero rates (Lab 3, Part B).

front: What are the payoffs of a call and a put at expiry, with strike K?
back: The call pays (S_τ − K)^+ and the put pays (K − S_τ)^+, where x^+ = max(x, 0) (Definition 1.1). The call is in the money when S_t > K, and the put when S_t < K.

front: What does the payoff identity (s − K)^+ − (K − s)^+ equal?
back: s − K for every real s (Lemma 1.2). A long call and a short put with the same strike and expiry therefore pay S_τ − K, the payoff of a long forward (Remark 1.3).

front: What is the difference between American and European exercise?
back: An American option may be exercised at any date t in [0, τ] for its intrinsic value h(S_t). A European option may be exercised only at expiry τ, as A5 states (Definition 2.1).

front: Under A2 and A3, how does the price of an American option compare with its intrinsic value?
back: V_A(t) ≥ h(S_t) at every date t (Proposition 2.2).

front: Under A2, A3 and A5, is an American option at date 0 worth at least the European option with the same terms?
back: Yes: V_A(0) ≥ V_E(0) (Proposition 2.3). The proof gives this weak inequality and nothing more.

front: On the SIMULATED path 100, 120, 90, 80, 110 USD, with strike 100 USD, expiry after four years and a one-year discount factor of 9/10, what is the date-0 value of holding the call to expiry?
back: 10(9/10)^4 = 6.561 USD, which is 6.56 USD to the cent (Example 2.5; Lab 1, Part 2).

front: On the Example 2.5 path, what is the put's best exercise date, and what is it worth at date 0?
back: Date 3, worth 20(9/10)^3 = 14.58 USD at date 0. Holding the put to expiry is worth 0 on this path (Example 2.5; Lab 1, Part 2).

front: What are the call and put break-even spots at expiry for the premiums of Lab 1?
back: Call 108 USD, the strike plus the 8 USD premium. Put 93 USD, the strike minus the 7 USD premium (Lab 1, Part 1).

front: Is an American option always worth more than its European counterpart?
back: No. Under A2, A3 and A5, Proposition 2.3 establishes only the weak inequality V_A(0) ≥ V_E(0). Strictness is not claimed for any put or call (Remark 2.4).

front: Should a call that is in the money be exercised at once?
back: Not as a rule. Under A2 and A3, exercise gives S_t − K, while selling the option gives its market value, which is at least S_t − K by Proposition 2.2. Exercising at once is therefore never better than selling at the market price.

front: Is the payoff at expiry the profit?
back: No. The profit subtracts the premium. In Lab 1 the call pays 25.00 USD at a spot of 125 USD, but its profit is 17.00 USD after the 8.00 USD premium (Lab 1, Part 1).

front: Is the best exercise date on a price path a trading rule?
back: No. Example 2.5 picks the best date after the path is known. A rule must choose the date from the prices observed so far (Remark 2.6).

front: What is the put-call parity identity for European options with strike K and expiry τ?
back: C − P = S − DK, with D = e^{−rτ} the discount factor (Definition 1.1).

front: Under A1 to A5, does put-call parity hold only at the money, or for every strike?
back: Every strike, not only the at-the-money one: C − P = S − e^{−rτ}K for every strike K > 0 (Theorem 1.2). The proof uses the four payoffs, A1, A2, A3 and A5 (no income, free short sales and lending, no arbitrage, and European exercise at expiry), and the rate of A4. It uses no distribution for S_τ (Remark 1.3).

front: What are the model-free option bounds?
back: Inequalities that European call and put prices must satisfy under A1 to A5 and (N), where (N) says the spot is non-negative at expiry. They use no model of how the spot is distributed (Definition 2.1).

front: Under A1 to A5 and (N), what range does a European call price C lie in?
back: 0 ≤ C ≤ S (Theorem 2.2(a)).

front: Which of the four model-free bounds use (N)?
back: Parts (a) and (c) use (N), because min(S_τ, K) is non-negative only when S_τ ≥ 0. Parts (b) and (d) do not use (N) (Remark 2.3).

front: What is convexity in strike, and what is the weight λ?
back: For strikes K1 < K2 < K3, with λ = (K3 − K2)/(K3 − K1), call prices satisfy convexity in strike at the triple if C(K2) ≤ λ C(K1) + (1 − λ) C(K3) (Definition 3.1). The word refers to strikes only.

front: Under A2, A3, A5 and (N), are European call prices convex in strike?
back: Yes, at every triple K1 < K2 < K3 with the same spot and expiry (Theorem 3.2). The proof is a payoff argument on the butterfly position, in four cases for S_τ.

front: Under A2, A3, A5 and (N), do call prices rise with strike?
back: No, they do not rise: C(K2) ≤ C(K1) whenever K1 < K2 (Corollary 3.4). The corollary gives no size for the fall.

front: Under A1 to A5, (N) and r ≥ 0, what is the date-0 price of an American call on an underlying with no income?
back: The same as the European call: V_A(0) = V_E(0) (Theorem 4.1). The equality holds at date 0 only. The equality V_A(t) = V_E(t) at a later date t is not established (Remark 4.2).

front: On the synthetic price set of Lab 1, what is the parity cost at each strike?
back: Zero at each of the five strikes, 80 to 120 USD (Lab 1).
basis: Lab 1 (SIMULATED price set; exact integer arithmetic)

front: What does a put raised by 300 cents at 100 USD do to the parity cost and to the parity payoff in Lab 1?
back: The parity cost at that strike is −300 cents. The parity payoff stays zero, because the payoff at expiry does not depend on the put price (Lab 1; Research R1).

front: When a call and a put at 90 USD are both raised by 500 cents in Lab 1, does put-call parity still hold?
back: Yes. The parity cost stays zero at every strike, because the call and the put rise by the same amount (Lab 1).

front: What are the evenly spaced second differences of the Lab 1 calls at 90, 100 and 110 USD?
back: 0, 100 and 800 cents. All three are non-negative as Theorem 3.2 requires, and the one at 90 USD is zero (Problem E1).

front: Does the early-exercise bound for a put imply that holding a put is worth at least its exercise value?
back: No. With K = 100, S_t = 50, one year left and r = 0.10, the put's bound is 100e^{−0.1} − 50 = 40.48 USD, below the 50 USD that exercise pays now (Section 5).

front: Is a call priced above the stock a bargain to buy?
back: No. Under A1 to A5 and (N), C ≤ S (Theorem 2.2(a)). If C were above S, selling the call and buying the share would have initial value S − C < 0 and payoff min(S_τ, K) ≥ 0 (uses (N)), which A3 excludes.

front: Does a convexity violation imply that one call is mispriced on its own?
back: No. Convexity in strike is a condition on a triple of strikes. In Lab 1 the planted error at 90 USD produces three violated triples, all sharing the same raised call (Lab 1).

front: Does Theorem 4.1 still give equal American and European call prices when the rate r is negative?
back: Theorem 4.1 does not cover r < 0. With r < 0 the bound in Theorem 2.2(b) can fall below S_t − K, so the step of the proof that uses r ≥ 0 fails (Remark 4.2; Problem R2).

front: What are the gross riskless return and the value today of a sure payoff of 1 at the end of the period?
back: R_f = 1 + r_1, where r_1 is the one-period rate, and a sure payoff of 1 is worth 1/R_f today (Definition 1.1). The unsubscripted r of A4 is not used in Lesson 6.

front: What are the stock's possible values in the one-period binomial model, and what does A6 require?
back: The stock is worth S_0 today and uS_0 or dS_0 at the end of the period. A6 requires 0 < d < R_f < u (Definition 1.2).

front: What does a replicating portfolio hold, and what equations does it satisfy?
back: Δ shares and a bond position B, where B > 0 is cash lent and B < 0 is cash borrowed. It satisfies Δ uS_0 + R_f B = V_1(u) and Δ dS_0 + R_f B = V_1(d). Its cost today is V_0 = Δ S_0 + B (Definition 1.3).

front: Under A1, A2, A3, A5 and A6, what is the cost of the one-period replicating portfolio?
back: V_0 = (q V_1(u) + (1 − q) V_1(d)) / R_f with q = (R_f − d)/(u − d), and 0 < q < 1 (Theorem 1.4(b)).

front: Under A1, A2, A3, A5 and A6, what happens if a claim trades at a price π different from the replicating cost V_0 in the one-period binomial model?
back: The price is not the replicating cost, so a zero-cost portfolio with a strictly positive payoff in every state exists, which A3 excludes; under A3 the price is V_0. If π > V_0, sell the claim, buy the replicating portfolio and lend the surplus; the total is (π − V_0) R_f > 0 in both states at zero cost. If π < V_0, reverse the positions (Theorem 1.4(c); Example 1.6).

front: In Example 1.5 (S_0 = K = 100, u = 3/2, d = 1/2, R_f = 5/4), what are the replicating shares and the bond position?
back: Δ = 1/2 share and B = −20 (borrowing 20) (Example 1.5).

front: Does the real-world probability of an up move enter the one-period price?
back: No. Under the hypotheses of Theorem 1.4, the formula in Theorem 1.4(b) uses u, d, R_f and the two payoffs. Two models with the same u, d and R_f but different up probabilities give the same V_0 (Remark 1.7).

front: What is the risk-neutral probability of an up move in the one-period binomial model?
back: q = (R_f − d)/(u − d), with Q(up) = q and Q(down) = 1 − q. Expectations under Q are written E^Q (Definition 2.1).

front: Under A1, A2, A3, A5 and A6, how is the one-period price written as an expectation?
back: V_0 = E^Q[V_1] / R_f, the discounted expectation of the payoff under Q (Theorem 2.2).

front: What is a recombining tree?
back: A tree in which an up move followed by a down move reaches the same node as a down move followed by an up move. Node (n, k) has stock price S(n, k) = S_0 u^k d^{n−k}, so there are n + 1 nodes at time n, not 2^n (Definition 3.1).

front: Is the risk-neutral probability q the probability that the stock goes up?
back: No. In Example 1.5, q = 3/4, while the stock's up factor is u = 3/2. q is the weight that makes the discounted expected payoff equal the replicating cost (Theorem 2.2; Definition 2.1).

front: What is backward induction on the recombining tree?
back: Set V(N, k) = f(S(N, k)) at expiry, and for n < N set V(n, k) = (q V(n+1, k+1) + (1 − q) V(n+1, k)) / R_f, with S(n, k) = S_0 u^k d^{n−k} (Definitions 3.1 and 3.2).

front: Under A1, A2, A3, A5, A6 and A6′, is the arbitrage-free price at each node of the multi-period tree given by backward induction?
back: Yes. The price at node (n, k) is V(n, k), the backward-induction value of Definition 3.2 (Theorem 3.3).

front: What is the two-period call price in Example 3.4 (the parameters of Example 1.5)?
back: V(0,0) = 45 currency units, that is 4500 cents at date 0 (Example 3.4; Lab 1: 45).

front: Does the self-financing strategy built from the time-0 holdings reproduce the claim on every path in Lab 1?
back: Yes, on the paths uu, ud, du and dd, and each node value is reproduced (Lab 1).

front: With next prices 150, 100 and 50 and only a stock and a bond to trade, can the payoff (1, 0, 0) be replicated?
back: No. The last two equations force Δ = 0 and R_f B = 0, and then the first equation reads 0 = 1 (Section 4). Replication depends on the payoff vector, not only on the number of states.

front: In Example 1.5, if the call trades at 35, what does selling it, buying 1/2 share and borrowing 20 leave today, and what does the position pay at expiry?
back: Cash of 35 − 50 + 20 = 5 today, lent at R_f = 5/4, so it pays 25/4 at expiry. With the sold call, the position pays 25/4 in both states at zero cost (Example 1.6).

front: Is the call's price the payoff at the expected final stock price, discounted?
back: No. The expected final price is 156.25, which discounts to S_0 = 100. The payoff at 156.25 is 56.25, and discounting it gives 36. The correct price is 45, the discounted expectation of the payoff (Theorem 3.3; Example 3.4).

front: What does Assumption A7 assume about the stock price and its volatility?
back: The terminal stock price is lognormal, its logarithm normally distributed, with a volatility σ > 0 that is constant over the life of the option and the same for every strike (Assumption A7). It is a model assumption, not a derived result.

front: How is the standard normal distribution function Φ written with the error function?
What is Φ(−x) in terms of Φ(x)?
back: Φ(−x) = 1 − Φ(x) for every real x (Lemma 1.2). The proof uses that the density is even and integrates to 1.

front: What is the Black–Scholes call formula of Lesson 7?
back: C = S Φ(d1) − K e^{−rτ} Φ(d2), with d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r + σ²/2)τ]/(σ√τ) and d2 = d1 − σ√τ (Definition 1.3).

front: How is the Black–Scholes put value written with Φ(−d1) and Φ(−d2), under A1 to A5, A7 and A8?
back: P = C − S + K e^{−rτ} = K e^{−rτ} Φ(−d2) − S Φ(−d1) (Proposition 1.4).

front: Under A7 and A8, on which inputs does the Black–Scholes call value depend?
back: Under the formula of Definition 1.3, C depends on S, K, rτ and σ√τ only, and not on the expected return of the stock (Proposition 1.5). The formula contains no drift term.

front: For n steps, what are the tree parameters u, d, R and q?
back: h = τ/n, u = e^{σ√h}, d = 1/u, R = e^{rh} and q = (R − d)/(u − d), with the same values at every node (Definition 2.1).

front: For r > 0 and σ > 0, when does 0 < d < R < u hold for the tree parameters?
back: If and only if h < σ²/r² (Lemma 2.2).

front: Under A1 to A5 and A7, with r > 0 and h < σ²/r², what is the n-step binomial call price?
back: V_n = e^{−rτ} Σ_{k=0}^{n} C(n, k) q^k (1 − q)^{n−k} max(S u^k d^{n−k} − K, 0) (Theorem 2.3). The discount factor e^{−rτ} equals R^{−n}, because nh = τ.

front: What is the pricing error e_n for n steps?
back: e_n = V_n − C, the tree price minus the Black–Scholes value, both in currency units (Definition 3.1).

front: In Lab 1, what is the Black–Scholes call value at spot 100, strike 100, r = 0.05, σ = 0.20 and τ = 1?
back: 10.450584 currency units, which is 1045 cents (Lab 1; Problem M2).

front: In Lab 1, what is the error at 2 steps, in cents?
back: −91 cents, from an unrounded error of −91.01 cents, so the tree price is below the closed form at 2 steps (Lab 1).

front: Does the binomial price approach the closed form from one side as the steps increase?
back: No. The error changes sign: it is positive at 1, 5 and 25 steps and negative at 2, 10, 50, 100, 200 and 400 steps. The nine values do not decide the limit.

front: In the Black–Scholes call, what does the numerator ln(S/K) + (r + σ²/2)τ reduce to when the σ² term is split as in Proposition 1.5?
back: d1 = (ln(S/K) + rτ)/(σ√τ) + σ√τ/2, so d1 uses only ln(S/K), rτ and σ√τ (Proposition 1.5).

front: Under A1 to A5, A7 and A8, does the put need its own formula, separate from the call?
back: No. Under A1 to A5, A7 and A8, Proposition 1.4 gives the put from the call and parity, and parity holds for the closed-form put in Lab 1 (Proposition 1.4; Lab 1).

front: For S = K = 100, r = 0.05, σ = 0.2 and τ = 1, what are d1 and d2?
For τ = 1, σ = 0.2 and r = 0.05, what are the four-step tree parameters u, d, R and q?
back: u = 1.105171, d = 0.904837, R = 1.012578 and q = 0.537808, and the condition h = 0.25 < σ²/r² = 16 holds (Problem M3).

front: What is the one-step tree price for S = K = 100, τ = 1, σ = 0.2 and r = 0.05?
back: u = e^{0.2} = 1.221403, q = 0.577493, and V_1 = 12.1623 currency units, which is 1216 cents. This matches Lab 1's first row (Problem E3).

front: In Lab 1, which step count has the smallest absolute error, and how large is it?
back: 400 steps, with an unrounded error of −0.0049977 currency units, which is −0.4998 cents and shown as 0 (Problem E1).

front: What is the put value for the M1 inputs?
back: P = 5.573526 currency units, which is 557 cents, from C − S + Ke^{−rτ} = 10.450584 − 100 + 95.122942 (Problem M2).

front: What is the implied volatility of an observed call price C*?
back: The number σ* > 0, if one exists, with C(σ*) = C*, where C(σ) is the Black–Scholes call value as a function of σ with S, K, r and τ fixed (Definition 1.1).

front: For S > 0, K > 0, τ > 0 and σ > 0, what is the derivative dC/dσ of the Black–Scholes call, and what does its sign imply?
back: dC/dσ = S φ(d1) √τ, which is positive for σ > 0. The call value is therefore strictly increasing in σ (Lemma 2.1).

front: For a fixed spot S > 0, strike K > 0, rate r and maturity τ > 0, what are the limits of the Black–Scholes call value as σ tends to infinity and to zero?
back: C(σ) → S as σ → ∞, and C(σ) → L = max(S − K e^{−rτ}, 0) as σ → 0⁺ (Lemma 2.2).

front: Under A1 to A5, A7 and A8 of Lesson 7, when does an implied volatility exist, and when is it unique?
back: It exists and is unique exactly when L < C* < S, where L = max(S − K e^{−rτ}, 0). If C* ≤ L or C* ≥ S, no volatility exists (Theorem 2.3, under A1 to A5, A7 and A8 of Lesson 7).

front: For the bisection of Definition 3.1, with C* in (L, S), a bracket of width W that satisfies its condition, and tolerance τ_tol, how many halvings are needed?
back: For a bracket with C(σ_lo) < C* ≤ C(σ_hi) and C* in (L, S), the first k with W/2^k ≤ τ_tol, which is ⌈log2(W/τ_tol)⌉ when W > τ_tol (Proposition 3.2).

front: What does the bisection of Definition 3.1 do at each step?
back: It tests the midpoint m against C* and keeps the half that still brackets C* (Definition 3.1).

front: For the bracket [10⁻⁶, 10] and tolerance 10⁻¹⁰, how many halvings does the procedure use?
back: 37. The width at 36 halvings is 10/2^36 = 1.46 × 10⁻¹⁰, still above the tolerance, and 37 halvings give a width below it (Problem M3). Lab 1 uses 37 halvings in every row.

front: For S = K = 100, r = 0.05 and τ = 1, what is the lower bound L?
back: L = 100 − 100e^{−0.05} = 4.8771, with the unrounded value 4.877058 (Problem M1).

front: Which of the prices 4.00, 4.90 and 100.00 at strike 100 has an implied volatility?
back: Only 4.90, which lies strictly between L = 4.8771 and S = 100. The price 4.00 is below L, and 100.00 equals the spot (Problem M2).

front: Does a successful inversion in Lab 1 establish that a quoted price is right?
back: No. The inversion starts from the formula's own price and returns the volatility that produced it, so it covers the inversion code and the formula only. No quote enters Lab 1 (Section 5).

front: What does Lab 1 do with a price outside the no-arbitrage bounds at strike 100?
back: It rejects the price with a message naming the no-arbitrage bounds, so no volatility is returned (Lab 1).

front: Is the implied volatility the stock's historical volatility?
back: No. Definition 1.1 uses the observed price, the spot, the strike, the rate, the maturity and the model. The stock's past prices do not enter.

front: At strike 120 with S = 100, r = 0.05 and τ = 1, what is the lower bound L?
back: 0, because 120e^{−0.05} = 114.15 exceeds the spot of 100, so S − Ke^{−rτ} is negative (Lab 1, Problem E2).

front: Under A1 to A5, (N) and r ≥ 0, does Theorem 4.1 give a rule for when an American call should be exercised early?
back: No. Theorem 4.1 gives a price equality at date 0 only, under A1 to A5, (N) and r ≥ 0. No rule is given for holding against exercising at a later date (Remark 4.2).

front: On the Example 2.5 path, what is the date-0 value of exercising the call at date 1?
back: 20 · 9/10 = 18.00 USD, the largest discounted intrinsic value on the path (Example 2.5; Lab 1, Part 2).

front: In Example 1.5, what is the cost of the replicating portfolio, in currency units?
back: V_0 = ΔS_0 + B = 50 − 20 = 30 currency units, which is 3000 cents and also (3/4 · 50)/(5/4) (Example 1.5).

front: In Example 3.4, what is the value after one up move, V(1,1), in currency units?
back: 75 currency units, from (3/4 · 125)/(5/4) = 75 (Example 3.4; Lab 1: 75).

front: In the market of Example 3.4 with the stock at 1/2, is the state price ψ_u positive?
back: No. ψ_u = (q − 9/10)/2 = −1/5 at q = 1/2, so the state prices are not both strictly positive and Proposition 3.2 does not apply (Example 3.4; Lab 1, Part B).

front: What does Assumption A1 (no income) of Lesson 2 say?
back: The asset pays no income, such as a dividend or a coupon, and bears no storage cost, between dates 0 and τ.

front: What does Assumption A2 (frictionless trading) of Lesson 2 permit and exclude?
back: It excludes transaction costs, bid–ask spreads and short-sale restrictions. An owner may sell the asset short and may lend or borrow any amount at the rate r of A4, with no default risk.

front: On which dates does Assumption A3 of Lesson 2 apply, for Proposition 2.2 and for Proposition 3.1?
back: For Proposition 2.2 it applies at dates 0 and τ, and for Proposition 3.1 at dates t and τ.

front: Under Assumption A3 of Lesson 4, what must a portfolio with initial value V_0 ≤ 0 and a non-negative payoff satisfy?
back: Its initial value and its payoff must both be zero: V_0 = 0 and X = 0 in every state. A3 is a hypothesis about markets, used in the proofs.

front: Under A4 of Lesson 4, what is the discount factor from date t to date τ?
back: e^{−r(τ − t)}, where the riskless rate r is constant over the life of the contract and compounded continuously (A4 of Lesson 4).

front: What is the annuity of a swap schedule, and where does it enter the par rate?
back: The annuity is the sum Σ_{i=1}^{n} DF_i of the discount factors over the payment dates. Under A8 it is the denominator of R_par = (1 − DF_n) / Σ DF_i (Proposition 3.3).

front: Is the Black–Scholes call formula derived in Lesson 7?
back: No. Assumption A8 takes it as the call value under A7, and it is used without derivation (Section 4).

front: Is Assumption A3 a fact that Lesson 1 establishes?
back: No. A3 is a hypothesis about the market, and a price set can violate it (Section 1; Lab 1, Part B).

front: In Example 3.4, what are the time-0 holdings of the replicating strategy?
back: 3/4 share and a bond position of −30, at cost 45 currency units (Lab 1).

front: What does assumption A6′ of Lesson 6 add to A6?
back: A6 holds at every node n < N with the same u, d and R_f, so the factors do not change from node to node (Definition 3.1).

front: Under A1, A2, A3, A5, A6 and A6′, what is the root price V(0, 0) as a sum over the paths of the tree?

For the bisection of Definition 3.1, started from a bracket with C(σ_lo) < C* ≤ C(σ_hi) and C* in (L, S), and stopped at tolerance τ_tol, how close is the reported midpoint to the implied volatility σ*?
back: Within τ_tol/2. The final bracket contains σ* and has width at most τ_tol, so its midpoint is within half that width (Proposition 3.2).

front: What bracket does the bisection of Definition 3.1 start from?
back: A bracket σ_lo < σ_hi with C(σ_lo) < C* and C(σ_hi) ≥ C* (Definition 3.1).

front: With evenly spaced strikes, what weight λ does the convexity condition use, and what does the condition reduce to?
back: λ = 1/2, and the condition reads C(K1) − 2C(K2) + C(K3) ≥ 0, a second difference of call prices on the strike grid (Remark 3.3).

front: Under A3, if portfolio a pays strictly more than b in every state, how do their costs compare?
back: p·a > p·b (Proposition 2.2, strict part). If the costs were equal, a − b would cost zero and pay a strictly positive amount in every state, which is an arbitrage opportunity that A3 excludes.

front: On the synthetic price set of Lab 1, does any model-free bound or convexity triple fail?
back: No. No model-free bound is violated, and no convexity triple is violated (Lab 1).
basis: Lab 1 (SIMULATED price set; exact integer arithmetic)

front: Do Propositions 2.2 and 2.3 of Lesson 4 need A1 (no income)?
back: No. Both use A2 and A3, and Proposition 2.3 also uses A5, so both hold whether or not the underlying pays income (Lesson 4, Section 3).

front: Under A2 of Lesson 4, may the options as well as the underlying be sold short?
back: Yes. A2 allows the underlying and the options to be sold short, and cash to be lent and borrowed at the riskless rate, with no transaction costs or bid–ask spread (A2 of Lesson 4).

front: Under A1 to A5 and (N), what is the lower bound on a European call price, with D = e^{−rτ}?
back: C ≥ max(S − DK, 0) (Theorem 2.2(b)). The maximum with zero makes the bound non-negative.

front: Under A1 to A5 and (N), what range does a European put price P lie in, with D = e^{−rτ}?
back: 0 ≤ P ≤ DK (Theorem 2.2(c)).

front: Under A1 to A5 and (N), what is the lower bound on a European put price, with D = e^{−rτ}?
back: P ≥ max(DK − S, 0) (Theorem 2.2(d)).

front: Under A1, A2, A3, A5 and A6, is the one-period replicating portfolio unique?
back: Yes, because u ≠ d and S_0 > 0 (Theorem 1.4(a)).

front: Are the state prices unique in the market of Example 3.4?
back: Yes. The two state-price equations have a nonzero determinant, −2, so there is one set of state prices. The lesson does not state uniqueness for other markets (Remark 3.3).

front: With a constant rate η per day on the margin account, does B_n equal F_n − F_0 for every price path?
back: For n ≥ 2 the identity holds for every price path only when η = 0, so A8′ is needed for Proposition 1.3 (Problem P3).

front: In the one-period binomial model, what does the call pay after an up move and after a down move?
back: max(uS_0 − K, 0) after an up move and max(dS_0 − K, 0) after a down move (Definition 1.2).

front: When does the bisection of Definition 3.1 stop, and what does it report?
back: It stops when the bracket width is at most τ_tol, and it reports the midpoint of the final bracket (Definition 3.1).

front: Under A1 to A4, if a forward is priced above F* = S e^{rτ}, which zero-cost portfolio is an arbitrage opportunity?
back: Sell the forward at F, buy one unit of the asset for S with a loan of S at rate r. The net cash flow today is zero, and the net payoff at expiry is F − S e^{rτ} > 0 in every state, which A3 excludes (Proposition 2.2, Case 1).

front: Under A1 to A4, if a forward is priced below F* = S e^{rτ}, which zero-cost portfolio is an arbitrage opportunity?
back: Buy the forward at F, sell one unit of the asset short for S, and lend S at rate r, which A2 allows. The net payoff at expiry is S e^{rτ} − F > 0 in every state, which A3 excludes (Proposition 2.2, Case 2).

front: Under A8′, what do the daily variation margins over days 1 to n sum to?
back: F_n − F_0, the settlement price minus the entry price (Proposition 1.3). The sum telescopes, and the proof needs no model of how the prices move.
basis: Proof on the page; Lab 3, Part A (SIMULATED path)

front: On the synthetic price set of Lab 1, how many (strike, expiry spot) pairs have a nonzero parity payoff?
back: None of the 40 pairs (Lab 1).
basis: Lab 1 (SIMULATED price set; exact integer arithmetic)

front: Under A1 to A4 and A3 at each date, is a forward that is fair at inception still worth zero after the spot moves?
back: No. Its value at date t is S_t − F* e^{−r(τ − t)}, which moves with the spot (Proposition 3.1; Remark 3.3; Lab 2, Part E).

front: Does the par-rate formula of Proposition 3.3 hold as written when a period is not one year?
back: Not as written. Each period is one year and no day count is used. An accrual factor other than one changes the formulas, and Remark 3.6 does not derive them.

front: What is a self-financing strategy?
back: A strategy that trades the stock and the bond at each node reached, where the holdings chosen at a node cost exactly the wealth carried to that node, so no cash is added or removed between dates (Definition 3.5).

front: Under Assumption A1 of Lesson 4, what does the underlying pay over the life of the contract?
back: Nothing: no dividend, coupon or storage cost (A1 of Lesson 4).
